questions.q: In the Victor Meyer test, propan-2-ol gives:
questions.explain: The 2° nitroalkane (CH₃)₂CH–NO₂ has one α-hydrogen; nitrosation gives the pseudonitrole (CH₃)₂C(NO₂)NO, whose blue colour is due to its C–N=O group (RBC: Red, Blue, Colourless).

questions.q: Why is silver nitrite, and not potassium nitrite, used to convert the alkyl iodide in the Victor Meyer test?
options: KNO₂ does not dissolve in organic solvents
AgNO₂ also oxidises the alkyl iodide to an aldehyde
KNO₂ attacks through oxygen and gives the alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O, which is useless for the test
AgNO₂ supplies the nitrous acid needed in the next step
questions.explain: Nitrite is an ambident nucleophile: AgNO₂ bonds through nitrogen to give the nitroalkane R–NO₂ that the test needs, while KNO₂ gives the alkyl nitrite.

questions.q: Why does 2-methylpropan-2-ol give no colour in the Victor Meyer test?
options: Its nitroalkane has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot be nitrosated by nitrous acid
It cannot be converted into an alkyl iodide by red P and I₂
Its nitrolic acid is colourless in NaOH
It is dehydrated by HNO₂ to an alkene
questions.explain: (CH₃)₃C–NO₂ has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing NO₂, so no nitronate forms and HNO₂ does not react; the solution stays colourless.

questions.q: Which alcohol gives a blood-red colour in the Victor Meyer test?
questions.explain: 2-Methylpropan-1-ol is primary (R–CH₂–OH); its nitroalkane has two α-hydrogens and forms a nitrolic acid whose sodium salt is red. The branching is a distractor: only the carbon bearing OH matters.
